Yes. She made a spreadsheet. With tabs. One of the tabs was labeled “Contingency: Rain.” There was a sub-tab.

Hannah and I met in second grade, when Mrs. Patterson assigned us to the same table and Hannah immediately reorganized our shared pencil box by color, then by length, then — and I want to be clear that this is a real memory — by “vibe.” I knew right then I had found my person. I also knew I would never again be allowed to hold a pencil without supervision.

Twenty-some years later, not much has changed. Hannah is the only person I’ve ever met who plans her spontaneity. She has a backup plan for her backup plan. When she called to tell me she was engaged — approximately forty-five minutes after it happened — she had already built a venue shortlist, a color palette, and a strongly worded document titled “Thoughts on Seating Charts.”

And here’s the beautiful part: none of that prepared her for Andrew.

Because Hannah had a plan for the proposal. It involved a mountain, a sunrise, a photographer, and — I am not making this up — a licensed drone operator. Instead, Andrew proposed in their living room, on a Tuesday, in sweatpants, halfway through assembling a bookshelf. He was holding an Allen key. There was a screw in his mouth. He said, “I can’t wait three more weeks. I’m doing it now.”

And Hannah — my friend who alphabetizes her spices — said yes before he finished the sentence.

That’s the thing about Andrew. He doesn’t fit neatly into a spreadsheet. He has this quiet, steady way of knocking every plan sideways and somehow making it better. The first time I met him, Hannah pulled me aside and warned me, “He’s a little quiet.” What she meant was: he’s the kind of quiet that actually listens. The kind of quiet that remembers you said, eight months ago, that your car makes a weird noise — and then shows up on a Saturday with a socket wrench and a donut.

He shows up. That’s Andrew. For the flu that flattened Hannah two winters ago, he drove four hours with soup in a cooler. For her grandmother’s recipe that she couldn’t get right, he spent a whole weekend burning pierogis until he did. He learned her family’s story because he wanted to be part of it — and then he became the part everyone asks about.

I have watched my best friend fall in love over these last few years, and I want to tell you what it actually looked like. It looked like Hannah laughing louder. It looked like her taking up space in a room without apologizing for it. It looked like her calling me and saying, “I don’t have to explain myself to him. He just gets it.”

And here’s the honest, slightly wobbly part of this speech, so bear with me.

When your best friend gets married, there’s this old, tired joke about losing her. I want to say, for the record, that I’m not losing anything. I’m gaining. I’m gaining a person who loves Hannah the way she deserves to be loved — stubbornly, patiently, on the ordinary Tuesdays, when nobody’s watching and there’s no drone operator in sight.

Because that’s what this is, isn’t it? It isn’t the mountain. It isn’t the sunrise. It’s the bookshelf. It’s the soup. It’s the person who sees you with the screw in your mouth and the Allen key in your hand and says, “This one. This is the one.”

Never go to bed angry. Go to bed with a snack — you’ll both feel better.

And never stop being curious about each other. Keep asking the questions. Keep choosing each other on the days that don’t make the photo album — because those are the days that make the marriage.

Andrew — welcome to the family. You’re in the group chat now. God help you.

*[Raise your glass.]*

So please, everyone, stand up and raise your glasses with me.

To Hannah and Andrew: may your love be like Hannah’s spreadsheets — carefully built, occasionally revised, and always, always adding up. And may your life together be one long, happy, beautifully unplanned Tuesday.

To the bride and groom!"}
